extracted.intended_audience: readers of Renaissance satire; students/scholars of Rabelais; general literary readers
extracted.subtask_description: Close reading of an English translation excerpt from Rabelais' Pantagruel (chapters on Panurge asking about marriage and various divination methods). Contains narrative, prescriptive statements, and procedural descriptions of divination practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virgilian lottery divination
rubrics_metrics.description: Bring hither Virgil’s poems, that after having opened the book, and with our fingers severed the leaves thereof three several times, we may, according to the number agreed upon betwixt ourselves, explore the future hap of your intended marriage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure and examples: open Virgil at random (sever leaves three times), select a line according to an agreed number; historic examples cited (Socrates, Alexander Severus, Adrian, Claudius, etc.) where verses supposedly foretold outcomes. Cautionary note appended: 'Do not you nevertheless imagine... that I would upon this kind of fortune-flinging proof infer an uncontrollable and not to be gainsaid infallibility of truth.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Homeric lottery divination
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequently by a Homeric lottery have many hit upon their destinies; as is testified in the person of Socrates... (examples of drawing verses from Homer to foresee events).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method similar to Virgilian lottery: consult Homeric verses at random to forecast fate; supported by anecdotal historical cases (e.g., Socrates, Brutus). Presented as an established custom but not necessarily infallible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dice and cockall gambling are deceitful and scandalous
rubrics_metrics.description: That sort of lottery is deceitful, abusive, illicitous, and exceedingly scandalous. Never trust in it. The accursed book of the Recreation of Dice... did of old... make many simple souls to err and fall into his snares.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong moral prohibition: Gargantua forbade dice across his dominions, caused moulds burned, suppressed the pastime as a dangerous plague to the state. Equates play-at-dice and cockall with devilish baited hooks that attract foolish souls to perdition. Anti-pattern: appealing to lone lucky examples (e.g., Tiberius) does not refute the prohibition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting a line using dice when divining
rubrics_metrics.description: Throw three dice upon this table... they fell so pat upon the lower points that the cast was five, six, and five. These are, sixteen in all. Let us take the sixteenth line of the page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical device for mapping chance to text: sum three dice to obtain a line number to read from the randomly opened page. Text gives concrete example (5+6+5 = 16 → 16th line). Also shows ceremonial trappings (nails awork, invoking deities optionally).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreting Virgilian lot verses for concrete outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific verses selected are read as portents: e.g., 'Nec Deus hunc mensa, Dea nec dignata cubili est.' interpreted as 'your wife shall be a strumpet, and yourself by consequence a cuckold.' 'Membra quatit, gelidusque coit formidine sanguis.' taken to mean 'she will soundly bang your back and belly.' 'Foemineo praedae, et spoliorum ardebat amore.' interpreted as 'she will steal your goods, and rob you.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrates how particular lines are given concrete, often negative, interpretations about marriage (cuckoldry, beating, theft). Also shows interpretive ambiguity: Panurge attempts contrary readings (e.g., reading 'steal' as playful theft of small tokens), illustrating that readings can be contested and are not objectively fixed.

rubrics_metrics.name: No appeal from decrees of Fortune (lots)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no appellation... from the decrees of fate or destiny, of lot or chance; as is recorded by our ancient lawyers... The reason hereof is, Fortune doth not acknowledge a superior, to whom an appeal may be made from her or any of her substitutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legalistic assertion used to close disputes over interpretation: once a lot or fate has spoken, according to the narrator, its decree is final and not subject to appeal. Cited authority (Baldus) and analogy to legal finality; presented as a cultural/legal convention in the narrative world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dream divination requires a skilled interpreter (oniropolist)
rubrics_metrics.description: For the better reading, explaining, and unfolding of these somniatory vaticinations... it is requisite for the better reading... that a dexterous, learned, skilful, wise, industrious, expert, rational, and peremptory expounder or interpreter be pitched upon, such a one as by the Greeks is called onirocrit, or oniropolist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims dreams can foretell events if certain physiological conditions exist (body at rest, well-nourished, concoction accomplished). Because the soul seldom reports visions perfectly due to frail senses, a learned interpreter is necessary. References classical authorities (Hippocrates, Plato, Aristotle, Artemidorus, etc.) to support method and legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of divination: do not infer infallibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not you nevertheless imagine... that I would upon this kind of fortune-flinging proof infer an uncontrollable and not to be gainsaid infallibility of truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The narrator warns readers not to treat divinatory methods (Homeric/Virgilian lottery, dice, dreams) as absolutely infallible. Though many anecdotes are given, the text explicitly cautions against overconfidence in such omens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulty of giving advice about marriage: individual resolve and fate matter
rubrics_metrics.description: The chief and main point of the whole matter lieth there. All the rest is merely casual, and totally dependeth upon the fatal disposition of the heavens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pantagruel refrains from categorical advice, arguing that whether to marry depends mainly on the individual's inner assurance and on fate; other arguments (debts, fear of cuckoldry, benefits of companionship) are 'merely casual'. Advises that if resolved, one should act rather than endlessly debate; suggests submission of outcome to God or chance if uncertain.
